newsitem.title: INDIA: U.N. chief urges India, Pakistan to push ahead.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief urges India, Pakistan to push ahead.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Saturday urged India and Pakistan to press ahead with bilateral talks, saying he was excited by the prospect of peace in the volatile region.
Annan met Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral at the start of a three-day visit to the Indian capital.
The United Nations chief said he had applauded India's efforts to smooth relations with its neighbours and welcomed the recent resumption of high-level peace talks with Pakistan.

"I think if we can defuse tensions in the region, reassure the people that they can live in security and shift resources from military to economic and social development, everybody would win," he told reporters after meeting Gujral.
Last month India and Pakistan resumed high-level talks that had broken off in early 1994 due to deep differences over the divided Himalayan region of Kashmir.
The two nations' foreign secretaries -- the highest-ranking civil servants in their foreign ministries -- ended four days of upbeat talks on March 31 and agreed to meet again in Islamabad.
But they failed to set dates, partly because of the political turmoil in New Delhi where Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda faces a vote of confidence in parliament on April 11.

Earlier this week, senior officials said they believed the political crisis in India would prevent Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Gohar Ayub Khan, from holding substantive discussions during meetings planned in New Delhi next week.

But Gujral told Reuters on Friday that the talks would go ahead as planned, and he would be seeing Khan on the sidelines of a meeting of foreign ministers of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) set for April 7-8, and after the conference.

On Saturday, before meeting Pakistani High Commissioner (ambassador) Ashraf Jahangir Qazi, Gujral told Reuters that no schedule of meetings with the Pakistani foreign minister had yet been set -- "but we will work it out".
A senior Foreign Ministry official said Gujral and Khan might hold talks on April 9, after the NAM conference ends.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.
Islamabad wants the United Nations to supervise a referendum of Kashmiris to determine whether the mostly Moslem region is folded into predominantly Hindu India or Islamic Pakistan.
But India says the matter is strictly a bilateral dispute and rejects any outside intervention.

Asked if he was more hopeful of progress in Indo-Pakistani talks after meeting Gujral, Annan replied: "It is going to take time. It is not going to be resolved overnight, but I think it is a wonderful initiative and I am really excited it is going on.
"I think from my sense the people of India support it," Annan said. "They want it, and I suspect it's the same in Pakistan and that the efforts will go on."
The secretary-general said he discussed the possible expansion of the U.N. Security Council with Gujral. India wants a permanent seat on an expanded council.

Annan said he also discussed nuclear disarmament. He told Reuters he did not see any contradiction between India's campaign for global nuclear disarmament and its opposition to the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) to ban nuclear tests.
But he said he considered the CTBT to be a step towards general disarmament.
Annan will address the NAM ministerial meeting on Monday.
